questions.commandDemand: Give the mechanism. Name the force and say what it does to the motion.
questions.stimulus: A ball is kicked straight up into the air. It slows down, stops for a moment, then falls back to the ground.
questions.stem: Explain the motion of the ball using the forces acting on it, from the moment it leaves the foot until it lands.

fuzzyTraps.precise: gravitational force acts on the ball, pulling it downwards towards the Earth
the gravitational force acting downwards slows the ball as it rises

chain.text: Gravitational force acts on the ball, pulling it downwards towards the Earth.
This force acts opposite to the motion, so the ball slows down.
The ball stops momentarily, but the gravitational force still acts on it.
The force now acts in the same direction as the motion, so the ball speeds up as it falls.

questions.modelAnswer: Gravitational force acts on the ball throughout, pulling it downwards towards the Earth. As the ball moves upwards this force acts in the opposite direction to its motion, so the ball slows down. At its highest point the ball stops moving for an instant, but the gravitational force is still acting on it, which is why it does not stay there. As the ball falls, the gravitational force now acts in the same direction as its motion, so the ball speeds up until it lands.
markPoints: Gravitational force acts downwards on the ball at all times
Rising: the force opposes the motion, so the ball slows down
At the highest point the ball is momentarily still but the force still acts
Falling: the force acts with the motion, so the ball speeds up
questions.whyMarksLost: The highest point is the mark most often missed. The ball is not force-free there; it is stationary for an instant while still being pulled down.

questions.commandDemand: Give the mechanism using surface area and the named force.
questions.stimulus: A parachutist jumps from a plane and falls quickly. When the parachute opens, he falls much more slowly.
questions.stem: Explain why the parachutist falls more slowly after the parachute opens, and explain why he eventually falls at a steady speed rather than continuing to slow down.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the parachute increases the surface area, increasing the air resistance acting upwards
air resistance acts upwards, opposing his downward motion

chain.text: The open parachute greatly increases the surface area moving through the air.
This increases the air resistance acting upwards.
The larger upward force opposes the downward gravitational force, so he slows down.
As he slows, air resistance falls until it balances the gravitational force, and he then falls at a steady speed.

questions.modelAnswer: When the parachute opens, the surface area moving through the air increases greatly, which increases the air resistance acting upwards on the parachutist. This larger upward force opposes the downward gravitational force, so he slows down. As he slows, the air resistance acting on him decreases, until it becomes equal to the gravitational force acting downwards. Once the two forces are balanced there is no overall force changing his speed, so he continues to fall at a steady speed.
markPoints: The parachute increases the surface area, increasing air resistance
Air resistance acts upwards, opposing the downward gravitational force
As he slows, air resistance decreases until it equals the gravitational force
With the forces balanced there is no change in speed, so he falls steadily
questions.whyMarksLost: Balanced forces mean no change in speed, not no motion. That distinction carries the last two marks.

questions.commandDemand: Read the data, state the conclusion, and say which rows you compared.
questions.stimulus:
A block was pulled across four different surfaces using a spring balance. The force needed to keep it moving was recorded.

Glass: 2.0 N
Wood: 3.5 N
Carpet: 6.0 N
Sandpaper: 8.5 N
questions.stem: What can you infer about the relationship between the surface and the frictional force? Explain how the data supports your answer.

fuzzyTraps.vague: rough things are harder to pull
fuzzyTraps.precise: the rougher the surface, the greater the frictional force acting on the block

chain.text: The rougher the surface, the greater the frictional force.
Glass, the smoothest surface, needed the smallest force at 2.0 N.
Sandpaper, the roughest surface, needed the largest force at 8.5 N.

questions.modelAnswer: The rougher the surface, the greater the frictional force acting on the block. Glass is the smoothest of the four surfaces and needed the smallest force of 2.0 N to keep the block moving, showing that the frictional force was smallest there. Sandpaper is the roughest surface and needed the largest force of 8.5 N, showing that the frictional force was greatest there. The force needed increases steadily from glass to sandpaper as the surfaces become rougher.
markPoints: The rougher the surface, the greater the frictional force
Evidence quoted from the smoothest surface with its value
Evidence quoted from the roughest surface with its value
The pulling force identified as a measure of the frictional force
questions.whyMarksLost: The spring balance measures the force needed to overcome friction, so the reading is the evidence. Saying only that it was 'harder to pull' never names what was measured.

questions.commandDemand: State the outcome and give the reason using the named force.
questions.stimulus: A toy car is rolled with the same push along a smooth tiled floor and then along a thick carpet.
questions.stem: Predict on which surface the car will travel further, and explain why.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the carpet is bumpy so it stops
fuzzyTraps.precise: the carpet is rougher, so a greater frictional force acts to oppose the car's motion

chain.text: The car will travel further on the smooth tiled floor.
The tiled floor is smoother than the carpet, so there is less frictional force.
Frictional force opposes the car's motion and slows it down, so less friction means the car travels further.

questions.modelAnswer: The car will travel further on the smooth tiled floor. The tiled floor is smoother than the thick carpet, so a smaller frictional force acts between the car's wheels and the surface. Frictional force acts in the opposite direction to the car's motion and slows it down, so with less friction the car takes longer to stop and travels a greater distance.
markPoints: The car travels further on the smooth tiled floor
Reason: smaller frictional force, which opposes the motion and slows the car
questions.whyMarksLost: The phrase opposes the motion is what makes this an explanation. Saying friction 'stops it' is a result, not a mechanism.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a workable change and explain it using a named force.
questions.stimulus: A bicycle chain squeaks and the pedals are hard to turn.
questions.stem: Suggest what could be done, and explain how it would help.

fuzzyTraps.vague: oil it so it runs smoothly
fuzzyTraps.precise: oil reduces the frictional force between the moving surfaces

chain.text: Apply oil to the chain.
The oil separates the moving surfaces so they do not rub directly against each other.
This reduces the frictional force, so less force is needed to turn the pedals.

questions.modelAnswer: Oil should be applied to the chain. The oil forms a layer between the moving metal surfaces so that they do not rub directly against each other. This reduces the frictional force acting between them, so less force is needed to turn the pedals and the squeaking stops.
markPoints: Apply oil or a lubricant to the chain
Explained as reducing the frictional force between the moving surfaces
questions.whyMarksLost: 'Makes it smoother' is the everyday phrasing. The mark is for naming the frictional force and saying it is reduced.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the effects a force can have.
questions.stimulus: A goalkeeper catches a fast moving ball. The ball stops, and the goalkeeper's gloves are pushed slightly out of shape.
questions.stem: Explain what the forces in this situation have done, naming two different effects a force can have.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the goalkeeper applies a force on the ball that stops its motion

chain.text: The goalkeeper applies a force that changes the ball's speed and stops its motion.
The ball applies a force on the gloves.
That force changes the shape of the gloves, so two different effects are on show.

questions.modelAnswer: The goalkeeper applies a force on the ball which acts in the opposite direction to its motion, changing its speed and bringing it to a stop. At the same time the ball applies a force on the gloves, and this force changes the shape of the gloves by pushing them out of shape. These are two different effects a force can have: it can change the motion of an object, and it can change the shape of an object.
markPoints: A force changes the speed of the ball and stops its motion
A force changes the shape of the gloves
Both are named as effects a force can have
questions.whyMarksLost: Two effects are on display and the question wants both named as effects, not just described.

questions.commandDemand: Give a similarity and a difference, mentioning both forces in each point.
questions.stem: Compare frictional force and gravitational force.

fuzzyTraps.vague: gravity pulls down and friction slows things
fuzzyTraps.precise: gravitational force always acts downwards towards the Earth, while frictional force always opposes the direction of motion

chain.text: Both are forces that can change the speed of an object.
Frictional force acts only when two surfaces are in contact and moving against each other.
Gravitational force acts on an object even without contact, always pulling it towards the Earth.

questions.modelAnswer: Both frictional force and gravitational force are forces that can change the speed of a moving object. However, frictional force acts only when two surfaces are in contact and moving against each other, and it always acts in the direction opposite to the motion. Gravitational force acts on an object without any contact being needed, and it always acts downwards towards the centre of the Earth.
markPoints: Similarity: both can change the speed of an object
Frictional force needs contact and always opposes the motion
Gravitational force needs no contact and always acts downwards towards the Earth
questions.whyMarksLost: Contact versus non contact is the sharpest difference and the one examiners reward. Direction alone is the weaker answer.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using poles and the rule of attraction and repulsion.
questions.stimulus: Two bar magnets are brought close together. In one arrangement they push apart. When one magnet is turned around, they pull together.
questions.stem: Explain these two observations.

fuzzyTraps.precise: like poles repel each other
unlike poles attract each other

chain.text: When the magnets pushed apart, like poles were facing each other.
Like poles repel each other.
After turning one magnet, unlike poles faced each other, and unlike poles attract.

questions.modelAnswer: When the magnets pushed apart, like poles were facing each other, for example north facing north. Like poles repel each other, so the magnets were pushed apart. When one magnet was turned around, unlike poles faced each other, for example north facing south. Unlike poles attract each other, so the magnets were pulled together.
markPoints: Like poles facing each other repel
Unlike poles facing each other attract
questions.whyMarksLost: The words like and unlike poles are the marks. 'Same' and 'opposite' ends are understood but are not the terms the mark scheme uses.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a decisive test and say what each result would prove.
questions.stimulus: A student has two identical looking steel bars. One is a magnet and one is not, but both are attracted to each other.
questions.stem: Suggest a test the student could carry out to find out which bar is the magnet, and explain what the result would show.

fuzzyTraps.vague: see which one is more magnetic
fuzzyTraps.precise: test for repulsion, because only two magnets can repel each other

chain.text: Bring one end of Bar A near one end of Bar B, then turn one bar around and repeat.
Repulsion happens only between two magnets; a magnet and a magnetic material can only attract.
If they never repel in any arrangement, only one of them is a magnet, and further tests with a known magnet identify which.

questions.modelAnswer: The student should bring an end of one bar close to the middle of the other bar. A magnet has its strongest attraction at its poles and almost none at its centre. If Bar A attracts Bar B when placed at Bar B's centre, then Bar A is the magnet, because a magnet attracts a magnetic material anywhere along its length, while a magnetic material is only attracted at the poles of a magnet. Repulsion is the other decisive test, because only two magnets can repel each other.
markPoints: A workable test using the centre of the bar or testing for repulsion
The key principle: only two magnets can repel each other
What each possible result would show
Why attraction alone cannot decide it
questions.whyMarksLost: Attraction proves nothing here because both bars attract either way. The fourth mark is for saying so explicitly.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using what happens to the magnet.
questions.stimulus: A magnet is dropped repeatedly on a hard floor and then heated strongly. Afterwards it picks up far fewer pins than before.
questions.stem: Explain why the magnet has become weaker, and suggest one way the magnet could be made stronger again.

fuzzyTraps.precise: dropping and heating disturb the arrangement inside the magnet

chain.text: The magnet has been dropped repeatedly and heated strongly.
Both disturb the orderly arrangement inside the magnet, reducing its strength.
It can be remagnetised by stroking with another magnet, always in the same direction.

questions.modelAnswer: Dropping a magnet repeatedly and heating it strongly both disturb the orderly arrangement of the magnetic material inside it. When this arrangement is disturbed, the magnetic strength of the magnet is reduced, so it exerts a smaller attractive force and picks up fewer pins. The magnet could be made stronger again by remagnetising it, for example by stroking it many times with one pole of another magnet, always in the same direction.
markPoints: Dropping and heating disturb the arrangement inside the magnet
This reduces its magnetic strength, so it attracts fewer pins
It could be remagnetised, for example by the stroking method or with an electromagnet
questions.whyMarksLost: Naming both causes from the stem matters, and the third mark rewards knowing the process is reversible.

questions.commandDemand: State the outcome and give the reason using the electromagnet's strength.
questions.stimulus:
An electromagnet was made by winding wire around an iron nail and connecting it to batteries. The number of paper clips it picked up was recorded.

1 battery, 20 turns of wire: 4 clips
1 battery, 40 turns of wire: 8 clips
2 batteries, 20 turns of wire: 9 clips
questions.stem: Predict how many paper clips the electromagnet would pick up with 2 batteries and 40 turns of wire, explain your reasoning, and state one thing that must be kept the same for the comparison to be fair.

fuzzyTraps.precise: more batteries increase the current, which increases the strength of the electromagnet

chain.text: Doubling the turns from 20 to 40 doubled the clips from 4 to 8.
Doubling the batteries from 1 to 2 raised the clips from 4 to 9.
Doing both should roughly double the strength again, to about 16 to 18 clips.
The same nail and the same size of paper clip must be used every time.

questions.modelAnswer: It would pick up roughly 16 to 18 paper clips. Increasing the turns of wire from 20 to 40 doubled the number of clips from 4 to 8, and increasing the batteries from 1 to 2 raised it from 4 to 9. Both changes increase the strength of the electromagnet, more turns of wire and a larger current each making it stronger, so applying both together should roughly double the strength again. For the comparison to be fair, the same iron nail and the same size of paper clips must be used in every test, so that only the turns of wire and the number of batteries change.
markPoints: A prediction of roughly 16 to 18 clips
Reasoning from the turns-of-wire pattern
Reasoning from the current pattern
A named variable kept the same, such as the nail or the paper clip size
questions.whyMarksLost: A bare number scores nothing. Two of the four marks are for reading the two separate patterns already in the table.

questions.commandDemand: State the steps in order.
questions.stem: Describe how a steel bar can be made into a magnet using the stroking method.

fuzzyTraps.precise: stroke the steel bar with one pole of a magnet, always in the same direction

chain.text: Place one pole of a magnet at one end of the steel bar.
Stroke the magnet along the bar in one direction, then lift it well clear before returning.
Repeat many times, always using the same pole and stroking in the same direction.

questions.modelAnswer: Place one pole of a magnet at one end of the steel bar. Stroke the magnet along the bar in one direction to the other end, then lift the magnet well clear of the bar before bringing it back to the starting point. Repeat this many times, always using the same pole and always stroking in the same direction. The steel bar will gradually become a magnet.
markPoints: Stroke with one pole of a magnet, always in the same direction
Lift the magnet clear between strokes and repeat many times
questions.whyMarksLost: Lifting the magnet clear between strokes is the detail that gets missed, and it is a mark. Dragging it back undoes the effect.

questions.commandDemand: Read the results and identify the materials, quoting the evidence.
questions.stimulus:
Four objects were tested with a magnet and the results recorded.

Object P: strongly attracted
Object Q: not attracted
Object R: strongly attracted, and also repelled when turned around
Object S: not attracted
questions.stem: Infer which object is a magnet and which are made of magnetic materials. Give your reasons, and explain why Object P cannot be a magnet.

fuzzyTraps.precise: R is a magnet, because only a magnet can be repelled by another magnet

chain.text: R was repelled as well as attracted, and only a magnet can be repelled by a magnet.
P was attracted but never repelled, so it is a magnetic material and not a magnet.
Neither was attracted, so neither is a magnetic material.

chain.step: Why P is not a magnet
chain.text: If P were a magnet, turning it round would have produced repulsion at some point.

questions.modelAnswer: Object R is a magnet, because it was repelled by the magnet when turned around, and only another magnet can be repelled. Object P is made of a magnetic material but is not itself a magnet, because it was attracted but never repelled. Objects Q and S are not made of magnetic materials, because they were not attracted at all. P cannot be a magnet because if it were, turning it around would have brought like poles together and produced repulsion at some point during the test; since only attraction was ever observed, P must be a magnetic material rather than a magnet.
markPoints: R identified as the magnet because it was repelled
P identified as a magnetic material because it was attracted but never repelled
Q and S identified as non-magnetic because they were not attracted
P cannot be a magnet because two magnets would repel in one orientation
questions.whyMarksLost: Repulsion is the only proof of a magnet, and this is the single most tested idea in the topic. Attraction never proves it.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a practical use and explain it using a property of the electromagnet.
questions.stimulus: A scrapyard needs to lift heavy pieces of iron and then release them into a container.
questions.stem: Suggest why an electromagnet is more suitable than a permanent magnet for this job.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the current can be switched off, so the magnetism stops and the load is released

chain.text: An electromagnet is only magnetic while a current flows through it.
Switching off the current removes the magnetism.
The iron is released into the container, which a permanent magnet could not do.

questions.modelAnswer: An electromagnet is magnetic only while an electric current flows through its coil. When the current is switched off, the electromagnet loses its magnetism and the iron it was holding is released into the container. A permanent magnet cannot be switched off, so the iron would stay attached to it and could not be dropped where it is wanted.
markPoints: An electromagnet is magnetic only while current flows through it
Switching off the current releases the load, which a permanent magnet cannot do
questions.whyMarksLost: The comparison with the permanent magnet is the second mark. Explaining only how an electromagnet works does not answer why it is more suitable.

questions.commandDemand: State what happens to each population and give the reason from the food chain.
questions.stimulus: A food chain in a field is: grass leads to rabbit leads to fox. A disease suddenly kills most of the rabbits.
questions.stem: Predict what will happen to the amount of grass and to the number of foxes, and explain why. Predict what will then happen to the rabbit population once the fox numbers have fallen.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the foxes have less food available, so their number decreases
fewer rabbits eat the grass, so the amount of grass increases

chain.text: Fewer rabbits eat the grass, so the amount of grass increases.
Rabbits are the foxes' food source, and there are far fewer, so fewer foxes survive.
With fewer foxes hunting them, and plenty of grass to eat, the surviving rabbits can increase again.

questions.modelAnswer: The amount of grass will increase, because there are far fewer rabbits left to feed on it. The number of foxes will decrease, because rabbits are the foxes' main food source and with far fewer rabbits many foxes will not obtain enough food to survive. Once the fox numbers have fallen, the surviving rabbits face less predation and have plenty of grass available, so the rabbit population will start to increase again.
markPoints: The amount of grass increases because fewer rabbits eat it
The number of foxes decreases because their food source has been reduced
The rabbit population then recovers
Because there is less predation and plenty of food available
questions.whyMarksLost: The recovery is what makes this a food chain rather than a list. Populations push back on each other in both directions.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the direction of energy transfer.
questions.stimulus: A student draws a food chain with the arrows pointing from the fox to the rabbit to the grass.
questions.stem: Explain why the arrows in the student's food chain are drawn the wrong way round, and state which way they should point.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the arrow means who eats who
fuzzyTraps.precise: the arrow shows the direction in which energy is transferred

chain.text: In a food chain the arrow shows the direction in which energy is transferred.
Energy passes from the grass to the rabbit when the rabbit eats the grass.
The arrows should therefore point from grass to rabbit to fox.

questions.modelAnswer: In a food chain the arrow shows the direction in which energy is transferred, and it should be read as is eaten by. Energy is transferred from the grass to the rabbit when the rabbit eats the grass, and from the rabbit to the fox when the fox eats the rabbit. The arrows should therefore point from the grass to the rabbit and then to the fox, which is the opposite of what the student has drawn.
markPoints: The arrow shows the direction of energy transfer, or means is eaten by
Energy passes from the grass to the rabbit to the fox
So the arrows should point grass to rabbit to fox
questions.whyMarksLost: The mark is for stating what the arrow means, not simply for redrawing it. This is a favourite examiner trap.

questions.commandDemand: Give the role of the organism in the habitat.
questions.stimulus: Fallen leaves and dead animals do not pile up endlessly on a forest floor.
questions.stem: Explain the role of decomposers in the forest, and predict what would happen to the forest if all the decomposers were removed.

fuzzyTraps.precise: they break down dead matter into simpler substances
they return nutrients to the soil for plants to use

chain.text: Decomposers break down dead plants and animals into simpler substances.
This returns nutrients to the soil for plants to absorb and use again.
Dead matter would pile up on the forest floor.
Nutrients would stay locked in it, so the soil would run short and plants would grow poorly.

questions.modelAnswer: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi feed on dead plants and animals and break them down into simpler substances, which prevents dead matter from accumulating on the forest floor. This also returns nutrients to the soil, where plants can absorb and use them again, so the nutrients are recycled within the habitat. If all the decomposers were removed, dead plants and animals would pile up and the nutrients inside them would stay locked away. The soil would gradually run short of nutrients, so the plants would grow poorly, and with fewer plants the animals that depend on them would decline too.
markPoints: Decomposers break down dead plants and animals
Nutrients are returned to the soil for plants to use again
Without them, dead matter would accumulate
Nutrients would not be returned, so soil quality and plant growth would fall
questions.whyMarksLost: The recycling of nutrients is the role; the pile-up is only the visible symptom. The prediction has to follow the nutrients, not just the mess.

questions.commandDemand: Read the food web and state the effect, tracing the path.
questions.stimulus: In a pond food web: algae are eaten by tadpoles and by small fish. Tadpoles are eaten by small fish and by dragonfly larvae. Small fish are eaten by herons.
questions.stem: Infer what would happen to the number of herons if a chemical killed all the algae. Explain your reasoning.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the number of herons decreases because their food source is reduced

chain.text: Algae are the producer and the food source for tadpoles and small fish.
Without algae, the numbers of tadpoles and small fish decrease.
Herons feed on small fish, so with fewer fish available the number of herons also decreases.

questions.modelAnswer: The number of herons would decrease. Algae are the producer in this food web and are the food source for both the tadpoles and the small fish. If all the algae are killed, the tadpoles and small fish will have no food and their numbers will fall. Herons feed on the small fish, so with far fewer fish available the herons will not be able to obtain enough food and their number will decrease as well.
markPoints: The number of herons decreases
Without algae the tadpoles and small fish decline, as algae are their food source
Herons feed on the small fish, so less food is available for them
questions.whyMarksLost: The middle of the chain is the mark. Jumping from algae straight to herons skips the reasoning.

questions.commandDemand: State the roles in order using the correct terms.
questions.stimulus: A food chain reads: lettuce, caterpillar, bird.
questions.stem: Describe the role of each organism in this food chain.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the lettuce is the producer, as it makes its own food

chain.text: The producer, because it makes its own food by photosynthesis.
A consumer that feeds on the producer, and prey for the bird.
A consumer and the predator of the caterpillar.

questions.modelAnswer: The lettuce is the producer, because it makes its own food by photosynthesis. The caterpillar is a consumer, because it cannot make its own food and feeds on the lettuce; it is also the prey of the bird. The bird is also a consumer, and it is the predator that hunts and eats the caterpillar.
markPoints: Lettuce identified as the producer that makes its own food
Caterpillar and bird identified as consumers, with predator and prey correctly assigned
questions.whyMarksLost: Producer and consumer are the core terms. Answers that say 'the lettuce gets eaten' describe the chain without using the vocabulary being tested.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a practical action and explain its effect on the habitat.
questions.stimulus: A mangrove swamp is being cleared to build houses. Conservationists want to protect it.
questions.stem: Suggest one reason why the mangrove swamp should be protected and explain it. Suggest one thing that could be done to protect it.

fuzzyTraps.vague: animals will have nowhere to live
fuzzyTraps.precise: the animals lose their habitat, which provides them with food and shelter

chain.text: The swamp is the habitat of many plants and animals.
It provides the food and shelter they need to survive.
It could be made a protected reserve so it cannot be cleared for building.

questions.modelAnswer: The mangrove swamp is the habitat of many plants and animals, providing them with the food and shelter they need to survive. If it is cleared, these organisms lose their source of food and their shelter, and many are adapted to live only in a mangrove habitat and would not survive elsewhere, so their numbers would fall and some species could die out completely. To protect it, the area could be made a nature reserve so that it cannot legally be cleared, and the houses could be built on land that is not a habitat for these species.
markPoints: The swamp is a habitat providing food and shelter
If cleared, the organisms cannot survive and numbers fall or species die out
A workable protection measure, such as making it a protected reserve or building elsewhere
questions.whyMarksLost: The third mark wants something practical and specific. 'People should care more' is not an action.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the amount of energy available at each level.
questions.stimulus: In a grassland there are about 10 000 grass plants, 500 grasshoppers, 40 frogs and 3 snakes.
questions.stem: Explain why the number of organisms decreases along the food chain, and explain why a food chain rarely has more than four or five stages.

fuzzyTraps.precise: only some of the energy is transferred at each stage of the food chain

chain.text: Energy is transferred along the food chain when one organism eats another.
Only part of the energy is passed on at each stage; the rest is used or lost.
Less energy is available further along, so fewer organisms can be supported.
After four or five stages so little energy remains that it cannot support another population.

questions.modelAnswer: Energy is transferred from one organism to the next along the food chain, but only part of the energy is passed on at each stage; the rest is used by the organism for its own life processes or lost to the surroundings. This means less energy is available at each successive stage, so fewer organisms can be supported further along the chain. A food chain rarely has more than four or five stages because by that point so little of the original energy remains that there is not enough to support another population of organisms at all.
markPoints: Only part of the energy is transferred at each stage
The rest is used by the organism or lost to the surroundings
Less energy further along means fewer organisms supported
Eventually too little energy remains to support another stage
questions.whyMarksLost: Size is not the reason. The whole answer is about how much energy is available, and the last mark asks you to follow that logic to its end.

questions.commandDemand: Give the mechanism by which the change causes harm.
questions.stimulus: A factory releases warm water into a river. Downstream, the number of fish falls sharply.
questions.stem: Explain how the warm water could cause the number of fish to fall, and suggest one thing the factory could do to reduce the harm.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the higher water temperature reduces the amount of dissolved oxygen in the water
the fish cannot obtain enough dissolved oxygen for respiration

chain.text: The warm water raises the temperature of the river.
Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen.
The fish cannot obtain enough oxygen for respiration, so many die or leave.
Cool the water before releasing it, or release it more slowly so the river warms less.

questions.modelAnswer: The warm water released by the factory raises the temperature of the river water. Warmer water is able to hold less dissolved oxygen than cooler water. The fish take in dissolved oxygen through their gills for respiration, so with less available they cannot obtain enough to survive, and many die or move away. To reduce the harm, the factory could cool the water down before releasing it into the river, or release it more slowly and in smaller amounts so that the river temperature rises far less.
markPoints: The warm water raises the river temperature
Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen
Fish cannot obtain enough oxygen for respiration, so they die or leave
A workable solution: cool the water first, or release it more slowly
questions.whyMarksLost: The dissolved oxygen step is the whole answer and the one most often skipped. Without it the answer is only 'it got too hot'.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the relationship between the two organisms.
questions.stimulus: A bee visits a flower to collect nectar. Pollen sticks to its body and is carried to the next flower.
questions.stem: Explain how both the bee and the flowering plant benefit from this interaction.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the bee obtains nectar as food, and the plant is pollinated

chain.text: The bee obtains nectar from the flower, which it uses as food.
Pollen sticks to the bee and is carried to another flower.
This brings about pollination, allowing the plant to reproduce.

questions.modelAnswer: The bee benefits because it obtains nectar from the flower, which it uses as a source of food. The plant benefits because pollen grains stick to the bee's body and are carried to the stigma of another flower. This brings about pollination, which the plant needs in order to reproduce and produce seeds. Both organisms therefore gain from the interaction.
markPoints: The bee obtains nectar as food
The plant is pollinated, allowing it to reproduce
questions.whyMarksLost: Each organism needs its own named benefit. 'They both get something' is the idea without the science.

questions.commandDemand: State the outcome and give the reason using competition.
questions.stimulus: A new species of fish that eats the same food as the native fish is released into a lake.
questions.stem: Predict what may happen to the native fish population and explain why. State one condition under which the two species could coexist instead.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the two species compete for the same food source

chain.text: The native fish population may decrease.
Both species feed on the same limited food source, so they compete.
If food were plentiful, or if the two fed on different things, there would be no competition.

questions.modelAnswer: The native fish population may decrease. Both species feed on the same food source and there is only a limited amount available in the lake, so the two species compete with each other for it. If the new species is better at obtaining that food, fewer native fish will get enough to survive and their numbers will fall. The two could coexist if the food supply were plentiful rather than limited, or if the new species fed on a different food, because then they would not be competing for the same resource.
markPoints: The native fish population may decrease
Reason: competition with the new species for the same limited food source
They could coexist if the food supply were not limited, or if the species fed on different foods
questions.whyMarksLost: Limited is the word that makes competition happen. The third mark checks you know that, by asking what would remove it.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a practical action and explain the effect it would have.
questions.stimulus: A river running through a town is polluted with rubbish and chemicals from nearby factories.
questions.stem: Suggest one action that could reduce the pollution, and explain how it would help the living things in the river.

fuzzyTraps.precise: treat the factory waste before it is released into the river

chain.text: Require factories to treat their waste before releasing it into the river.
This removes harmful chemicals so they do not enter the water.
The water quality improves, so plants and animals in the river can survive and their numbers recover.

questions.modelAnswer: Factories could be required to treat their waste to remove harmful chemicals before releasing it into the river. This would prevent harmful substances from entering the water, so the water quality would improve. The plants and animals living in the river would then be able to survive in their habitat, and their numbers could recover.
markPoints: A practical action to reduce pollution entering the river
Explained as improving conditions so the organisms in the habitat can survive
questions.whyMarksLost: The second half is often left out. Every suggest question about the environment wants the effect on the living things, not just the action.

questions.commandDemand: Read the data and state what it shows, quoting figures.
questions.stimulus:
The number of a certain insect and the number of the birds that eat them were counted in a woodland over four years.

Year 1: 8000 insects, 120 birds
Year 2: 3000 insects, 130 birds
Year 3: 2000 insects, 70 birds
Year 4: 6000 insects, 50 birds
questions.stem: What can you infer about the relationship between the insect and bird populations?

fuzzyTraps.vague: they go up and down together
fuzzyTraps.precise: changes in the prey population are followed by changes in the predator population

chain.text: The birds are the predators and the insects are their prey.
The insects fell from 8000 to 2000 by Year 3, and the birds then fell from 130 to 70.
By Year 4, with fewer birds, the insect number rose again to 6000.

questions.modelAnswer: The birds are the predators and the insects are their prey, and each population affects the other. When the insect number fell from 8000 in Year 1 to 2000 in Year 3, the bird number then fell from 130 to 70, because there was less food available for the birds. In Year 4 there were only 50 birds, so fewer insects were eaten and the insect number rose again to 6000. Changes in the prey population are followed by changes in the predator population.
markPoints: Predator and prey relationship identified, with birds eating insects
A fall in the prey population is followed by a fall in the predator population
Supported with figures from the table
With fewer predators the prey population then recovers, supported by Year 4
questions.whyMarksLost: The populations do not move together; the predator responds after the prey. Year 4 is in the table to show the recovery, and it carries a mark.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the effect on the food chain.
questions.stimulus: Farmers spray a pesticide on their crops to kill insect pests. Some of the pesticide remains on the plants.
questions.stem: Explain how this pesticide could harm birds that do not eat the crops, and explain why the birds are harmed even though each insect carries only a tiny amount.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the pesticide is passed along the food chain and builds up in the birds

chain.text: Insects feed on the sprayed crops and take in the pesticide.
Birds eat these insects, so the pesticide passes along the food chain.
Each bird eats a large number of insects, so the pesticide builds up in its body.
Many tiny amounts together reach a level that is harmful to the bird.

questions.modelAnswer: The insects feed on the sprayed crops and take in the pesticide. Birds that eat these insects take in the pesticide inside them, so it is passed along the food chain even though the birds never eat the crops. Each bird eats a very large number of insects over time, and the pesticide is not removed from its body, so it accumulates. Many tiny amounts together build up to a level that is harmful, which is why the birds are affected although each individual insect carried only a trace.
markPoints: The pesticide passes along the food chain from crops to insects to birds
Each bird eats a large number of insects
The pesticide accumulates in the bird's body rather than being removed
The built-up amount reaches a harmful level
questions.whyMarksLost: Accumulation is the whole point and is worth two of the four marks. Without it there is no reason a trace amount should matter.

questions.commandDemand: State the interactions taking place. Name each type.
questions.stimulus: In a garden, caterpillars eat leaves, birds eat caterpillars, and two rose bushes planted close together both grow poorly.
questions.stem: Describe two different types of interaction taking place in this garden.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the two rose bushes compete for water, mineral salts and sunlight

chain.text: The birds are predators and the caterpillars are their prey.
The two rose bushes compete with each other.
They compete for limited water, mineral salts and sunlight, so both grow poorly.

questions.modelAnswer: The first interaction is a predator and prey relationship: the birds are predators that hunt and eat the caterpillars, which are their prey. The second interaction is competition: the two rose bushes are planted close together and compete with each other for limited water, mineral salts and sunlight, which is why both of them grow poorly.
markPoints: Predator and prey interaction identified between the birds and caterpillars
Competition identified between the rose bushes, with the resources named
questions.whyMarksLost: Both interactions must be named with the correct term. Describing what happens without the words predator, prey or competition scores poorly.

questions.commandDemand: Link the structure to how it helps the organism survive.
questions.stimulus: A desert plant has thick fleshy stems, and leaves that are reduced to thin spines.
questions.stem: Explain how these two features help the plant survive in the desert.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the spines stop animals eating it
fuzzyTraps.precise: the spines have a small surface area, which reduces water loss
the thick fleshy stem stores water for use when there is no rain

chain.text: The thick fleshy stem stores water.
The plant can use this stored water during long periods without rain.
The spines have a very small surface area.
This reduces the amount of water lost from the plant.

questions.modelAnswer: The thick fleshy stem stores water inside the plant. This allows the plant to survive during the long periods without rain in the desert, because it can use the stored water. The leaves are reduced to thin spines, which have a very small surface area. This greatly reduces the amount of water lost from the plant, so the plant conserves the water it has.
markPoints: The fleshy stem stores water for use when there is no rain
The spines have a small surface area, reducing water loss
Both features named as adaptations to a habitat with very little water
Each linked explicitly to surviving in the desert
questions.whyMarksLost: Two features are named in the stem, so two benefits are wanted, and every adaptation answer must end at survival in that habitat.

questions.commandDemand: Link the feature to survival, naming the advantage.
questions.stimulus: A stick insect has a long thin brown body that looks almost exactly like a twig.
questions.stem: Explain how this appearance helps the stick insect to survive.

fuzzyTraps.precise: it is camouflaged, so predators are less likely to see it

chain.text: Its body resembles a twig in shape and colour.
This camouflages it against the branches, so it blends in with its surroundings.
Predators are less likely to spot and eat it, so it is more likely to survive.

questions.modelAnswer: The stick insect's long thin brown body resembles a twig in both shape and colour. This camouflages the insect against the branches of the plant so that it blends in with its surroundings. Predators are therefore less likely to notice and catch it, so the stick insect has a greater chance of surviving to reproduce.
markPoints: The insect is camouflaged and blends in with its surroundings
Predators are less likely to see it, so it is more likely to survive
questions.whyMarksLost: The word camouflage and the mention of predators are both needed. Saying 'it looks like a twig' repeats the stem without explaining the advantage.

questions.commandDemand: State what happens and explain using the advantage of the adaptation.
questions.stimulus: A population of moths lives on pale tree bark. Most are pale, but a few are dark. Pollution then turns the tree bark dark.
questions.stem: Predict what will happen to the numbers of pale and dark moths, and explain why. Explain also why individual moths do not change colour to match the darkened bark.

fuzzyTraps.precise: individual moths do not change; the proportion of dark moths in the population increases

chain.text: They are now easily seen against the dark bark, so more are eaten and their numbers fall.
They are now camouflaged, so fewer are eaten.
More dark moths survive to reproduce, so their numbers rise.
Colour is inherited, and an individual cannot change it during its lifetime.
What changes is the proportion of each colour in the population, not any individual moth.

questions.modelAnswer: The number of pale moths will decrease and the number of dark moths will increase. On the darkened bark the pale moths are no longer camouflaged and stand out clearly, so predators can see and eat more of them, while the dark moths are now camouflaged against the bark and are less likely to be spotted. More dark moths therefore survive to reproduce and pass on their colour. Individual moths do not change colour to match the bark, because colour is an inherited characteristic and an individual cannot change its inherited features during its lifetime. What changes over time is the proportion of dark and pale moths in the population, because of which ones survive long enough to reproduce.
markPoints: Pale moths decrease and dark moths increase
Pale moths are no longer camouflaged so more are eaten by predators
Dark moths are camouflaged so more survive to reproduce
Colour is inherited and cannot be changed within an individual's lifetime
It is the proportion in the population that changes, not any individual
questions.whyMarksLost: Writing that the moths change colour to match the bark is the classic error and now costs two marks, because two of the five are specifically about why that cannot happen.

questions.commandDemand: Read the features and infer the habitat, giving the evidence.
questions.stimulus: An animal has the following features: a thick layer of fat under its skin, a dense white coat, and broad feet with fur on the soles.
questions.stem: Infer the habitat this animal is adapted to live in, and explain how each feature helps it.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the fat layer insulates the body, reducing heat loss to the cold surroundings

chain.text: The animal is adapted to a very cold, snowy habitat.
The fat layer and dense coat insulate the body and reduce heat loss to the cold surroundings.
The white coat camouflages it against the snow, and broad feet spread its weight over the snow.

questions.modelAnswer: The animal is adapted to live in a very cold, snowy habitat. The thick layer of fat and the dense coat both insulate its body, reducing the loss of heat energy to the cold surroundings so that it stays warm. The white coat camouflages it against the snow, making it harder for predators or prey to see it. Its broad feet spread its weight over a larger surface area so it does not sink into the snow.
markPoints: Habitat identified as very cold or snowy
The fat layer and dense coat insulate, reducing heat loss to the cold surroundings
The white coat camouflages it against the snow
Broad furry feet spread its weight so it does not sink into the snow
questions.whyMarksLost: The fat does not make heat; it reduces heat loss. Examiners look for the word insulate or the phrase reduce heat loss.

questions.commandDemand: State a similarity and a difference, referring to both plants in each point.
questions.stimulus: A water lily has broad flat leaves that float on the surface. A cactus has leaves reduced to spines.
questions.stem: Compare how the leaves of these two plants are adapted to their habitats.

fuzzyTraps.vague: one has big leaves and one has small
fuzzyTraps.precise: the large surface area absorbs more sunlight, while the small surface area reduces water loss

chain.text: Both have leaves adapted to help the plant survive in its own habitat.
Broad flat leaves have a large surface area to absorb more sunlight for photosynthesis, and water is plentiful.
Spines have a very small surface area, which reduces water loss where water is scarce.

questions.modelAnswer: Both plants have leaves that are adapted to help them survive in their own habitat. However, the water lily has broad flat leaves with a large surface area, which absorb more sunlight for photosynthesis and float on the surface where water is plentiful. The cactus has leaves reduced to spines with a very small surface area, which greatly reduces the water lost from the plant, because water is scarce in the desert.
markPoints: Similarity: both have leaves adapted to their habitat
Water lily: large surface area to absorb more sunlight, where water is plentiful
Cactus: very small surface area to reduce water loss, where water is scarce
questions.whyMarksLost: Surface area is the single idea connecting both halves. An answer that never uses the phrase is describing the leaves, not comparing the adaptations.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a feature and explain the advantage it gives.
questions.stimulus: A newly discovered fish lives at the very bottom of the deep ocean, where no sunlight reaches and food is scarce.
questions.stem: Suggest one feature this fish might have, and explain how it would help the fish survive there.

fuzzyTraps.vague: it can see in the dark
fuzzyTraps.precise: it has very large eyes to detect the small amount of light available, or it produces its own light

chain.text: The fish might produce its own light from part of its body.
In complete darkness this light attracts prey towards it.
The fish can catch food more easily where food is scarce, so it is more likely to survive.

questions.modelAnswer: The fish might have a part of its body that produces its own light. In the deep ocean no sunlight reaches the sea bed, so it is completely dark. The light produced would attract other small animals towards the fish, allowing it to catch prey more easily in a place where food is scarce. This would increase its chance of obtaining enough food to survive.
markPoints: A sensible feature suited to darkness or scarce food
Explained as helping the fish obtain food or detect its surroundings, so it survives
questions.whyMarksLost: Suggest questions accept several answers, but every answer must end at survival. A feature with no stated advantage scores one mark at most.

questions.commandDemand: State the features and what each one does.
questions.stimulus: A mangrove tree grows in soft waterlogged mud beside the sea, where the water is salty.
questions.stem: Describe three adaptations a mangrove tree may have, state how each helps it, and explain which single feature of the habitat makes breathing roots necessary.

fuzzyTraps.precise: prop roots spread outwards to support the tree in the soft mud

chain.text: Prop roots spread outwards to support the tree in soft, unstable mud.
Breathing roots grow upwards above the mud to take in oxygen from the air.
Leaves can remove excess salt, so the tree survives in salty water.
The mud is waterlogged, so it contains very little oxygen for the roots to use.

questions.modelAnswer: A mangrove tree may have prop roots that spread widely from the trunk, supporting the tree so it does not fall over in the soft, unstable mud. It may have breathing roots that grow upwards out of the mud, which take in oxygen directly from the air. It may also have leaves that remove excess salt, which allows the tree to survive even though the water around it is salty. Breathing roots are necessary because the mud is waterlogged: water fills the spaces between the mud particles, so there is very little oxygen in the mud itself for the roots to take in, and the tree must obtain it from the air above instead.
markPoints: Prop roots for support in soft mud
Breathing roots to take in oxygen from the air
A way of dealing with salt, such as removing it through the leaves
The mud is waterlogged
So it contains very little oxygen, which is why oxygen must come from the air
questions.whyMarksLost: The last two marks are the reason behind the adaptation. Waterlogged mud has almost no oxygen in it, and that single fact is what makes breathing roots necessary.
